lessons.title: Get ready! What you will learn

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📊 **Strand 4 — Handling Data**
Collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting information to make good decisions.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.4.1)
- B9.4.1.2 — Select, justify and use appropriate methods of collecting data (quantitative and qualitative), organise and analyse the data, and interpret the results using descriptive statistics (measures of central tendency and range).

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- recognise how bias (language, ethics, cost, time and timing, privacy, cultural sensitivity) can influence data
- write fair, unbiased survey questions
- calculate the minimum, maximum, range, mean, median and mode, and use them to make decisions
- describe the effect of extreme values on the mean, median and mode

lessons.title: Bias in data collection

pages.title: Bias in data collection
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Select a method for collecting data, taking into consideration how bias (use of language, ethics, cost, time and timing, privacy or cultural sensitivity) may influence data.
Curriculum indicator B9.4.1.2.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Bias** — **Bias** is anything in the way data are collected that pushes the results in one direction, so that they do not fairly represent the truth.
| **Source of bias** | **Example** | **How to avoid it** |
|---|---|---|
| Language (leading questions) | "Don't you think the teaching of mathematics is very good?" | Use neutral wording and balanced answer choices |
| Choice of respondents (sample) | Asking only footballers about sports injuries | Ask a fair (random, varied) sample |
| Ethics | Using answers for a purpose not told to respondents | Explain honestly how data will be used; get consent |
| Time and timing | Asking about rainfall only in the rainy season | Collect data over a suitable period |
| Privacy | "What is your current body weight?" in a class survey | Make sensitive questions optional or anonymous |
| Cultural sensitivity | "Tick your favourite method of cooking pork" | Make questions apply to everyone (some people do not eat pork) |
| Cost | Surveying only nearby schools to save money | Plan a budget that allows a fair sample |

pages.title: Example 14.1
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 14.1
A school survey form asked: "Overall, don't you think the teaching of mathematics is very good?" Explain the bias and suggest a better question.
**Solution**
The wording **leads** respondents to answer "yes" — it shows the writer's opinion and offers only yes/no.
A better question: "Overall, how would you rate the teaching of mathematics?" □ Very poor □ Poor □ Fair □ Good □ Very good
## ✏️ Example 14.2
Ama Mereku in B9 wants to write an article on sport-related injuries for the school magazine. She collects responses only from the school football team. Identify the influencing factors and how she can report more accurately.
**Solution**
The factors are **bias in the sample** and **time**. Football is a contact sport, so footballers are likely to report many injuries — the results will overstate injuries in sport generally. Ama should take **more time** to ask a wider sample, including learners who do contact and non-contact sports (athletics, tennis, volleyball and so on).

pages.title: Example 14.3
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 14.3
a) A physical education teacher's survey on "Overall Physical Health" asks: "What is your current body weight?" Identify the influencing factor and give a solution. b) You tell classmates their answers to "What is your worst subject?" are for planning remedial classes, but then use them in a magazine article. How would this be described, and how would it affect future surveys? c) A questionnaire asks people to tick their favourite method of cooking pork. What is wrong, and how can it be improved?
**Solution**
a) **Privacy**: some learners may feel embarrassed to give their weight, so they may not answer or may give false values. Solution: make the question optional, collect it anonymously, or ask for a weight **range** (e.g. 40–49 kg).
b) This is **unethical** — the data are used for a purpose different from the one stated, without permission. Classmates will lose trust and may refuse to answer, or answer dishonestly, in future surveys.
c) It is **not culturally sensitive** — it assumes everyone eats pork. Better: "If you eat pork, please tick your favourite method of cooking it: □ Boiling □ Grilling □ Frying" (with the question marked optional).

pages.title: Exercise 14.1
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 14.1** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Rewrite each question to remove the bias: a) "Do you agree that our headteacher is the best in the district?" b) "How much money did your parents earn last year?" c) "Which church do you attend on Sundays?"
2. A survey on the quality of school meals was carried out by asking learners standing in the queue for second helpings. Explain the bias.

questions.q: Rewrite each question to remove the bias:

parts.q: (a) "Do you agree that our headteacher is the best in the district?"
parts.a: "How would you rate the headteacher's leadership? (Very poor … Very good)"

parts.q: (b) "How much money did your parents earn last year?"
parts.a: Make it optional and use income ranges, or remove it if it is not needed.

parts.q: (c) "Which church do you attend on Sundays?"
parts.a: "Do you belong to a religious group? If so, which one? (optional)" — it should not assume that everyone is Christian.

questions.q: A survey on the quality of school meals was carried out by asking learners standing in the queue for second helpings. Explain the bias.

parts.a: Learners asking for more food probably like the meals, so the results will be too favourable (sample bias).

pages.title: Descriptive statistics
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Organise and analyse data and interpret the results using descriptive statistics (minimum, maximum, measures of central tendency and range) to answer a given question.
Curriculum indicator B9.4.1.2.2
## ✏️ Example 14.4
Use the lifespans of the 30 bulbs in Chapter 13 (Section 13.2). Find: a) the minimum b) the maximum c) the range d) the mean e) the median f) the mode. g) When ordering bulbs of this type for your shop, what would you consider?
**Solution**
a) Minimum = **164 hours** b) Maximum = **178 hours** c) Range = 178 − 164 = **14 hours**
d) Sum of the 30 lifespans = 5,151 hours. Mean = [[5151/30]] = **171.7 hours**
e) Median = **172 hours** (15th and 16th values) f) Mode = **173 hours**
g) The bulbs are consistent (small range of 14 hours), and a typical bulb lasts about 172 hours. A shopkeeper might advertise "about 170 hours" and compare price per hour of light with other brands before ordering.

pages.title: Exercise 14.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 14.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. The daily sales (GH₵) of a provision shop for 10 days were: 245, 310, 280, 295, 260, 310, 275, 330, 290, 305. Find the minimum, maximum, range, mean, median and mode.
2. Two brands of batteries were tested (hours): Brand A: 10, 11, 10, 12, 11, 10, 11; Brand B: 6, 15, 9, 14, 12, 8, 13. Compare the brands using the mean and range. Which would you buy? Why?

questions.q: The daily sales (GH₵) of a provision shop for 10 days were: 245, 310, 280, 295, 260, 310, 275, 330, 290, 305. Find the minimum, maximum, range, mean, median and mode.

parts.a: Min 245, max 330, range 85, mean 290, median 292.5, mode 310

questions.q: Two brands of batteries were tested (hours): Brand A: 10, 11, 10, 12, 11, 10, 11; Brand B: 6, 15, 9, 14, 12, 8, 13. Compare the brands using the mean and range. Which would you buy? Why?

parts.a: A: mean 10.7, range 2; B: mean 11, range 9. Brand A — slightly lower mean but far more consistent (reliable).

lessons.title: The effect of extreme values

pages.title: The effect of extreme values
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Demonstrate the effect on the mean, median and mode when extreme data are included in a data set.
Curriculum indicator B9.4.1.2.3
## ✏️ Example 14.5
Use the bulb data (mean 171.7 h, median 172 h, mode 173 h).
a) One bulb (the 178-hour bulb) is replaced by a new bulb with a lifespan of 300 hours. Find the new mean and compare. b) Instead, the 164-hour bulb is replaced by one lasting only 70 hours. Find the new mean and compare. c) What happens to the median and mode in each case?
**Solution**
a) New sum = 5,151 − 178 + 300 = 5,273. New mean = [[5273/30]] ≈ **175.8 hours** — up by about 4 hours.
b) New sum = 5,151 − 164 + 70 = 5,057. New mean = [[5057/30]] ≈ **168.6 hours** — down by about 3 hours.
c) In both cases the **median stays 172** and the **mode stays 173**: one extreme value does not change the middle position or the most common value.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Effect of extreme values** — An **extreme value (outlier)** changes the **mean** noticeably (a large value pulls it up, a small value pulls it down) and greatly increases the **range**. The **median** and **mode** are usually little affected. When data contain extreme values, the median is often the better average to report.
> 🧪 **Activity 14.1 — Investigate extreme values**
In small groups, keep replacing values in the bulb data with extreme values (very small and very large). Each time, calculate the mean, median, mode and range. Record your results in a table and write two conclusions.

pages.title: Exercise 14.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 14.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. The ages of 6 people at a meeting are 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 15. Find the mean, median and mode. A 75-year-old grandfather joins them. Find the new mean, median and mode. Which average best describes the group now?
2. Kofi's test marks are 65, 70, 68, 72 and 4 (he was ill for one test). Calculate the mean with and without the 4. Which better reflects his ability?

questions.q: The ages of 6 people at a meeting are 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 15. Find the mean, median and mode. A 75-year-old grandfather joins them. Find the new mean, median and mode. Which average best describes the group now?

parts.a: Before: mean 15.3, median 15, mode 15. After: mean 23.9, median 15, mode 15. The median (or mode) — the mean is distorted by the single extreme age.

questions.q: Kofi's test marks are 65, 70, 68, 72 and 4 (he was ill for one test). Calculate the mean with and without the 4. Which better reflects his ability?

parts.a: With: 55.8; without: 68.75. The mean without the 4 (or the median, 68) better reflects his ability.

lessons.title: Chapter summary

pages.title: Chapter 14 summary
pages.body:
- Bias comes from leading language, unfair samples, unethical use of data, poor timing, intrusive (private) or culturally insensitive questions, and cost-cutting.
- Descriptive statistics: minimum, maximum, range, mean, median, mode.
- Extreme values strongly affect the mean and range, but hardly the median and mode.
